title: Single-cell Multiomics
text:
Overview of lesson
Before designing an experiment and collecting samples, it is important to determine which assays will be most beneficial to answering your biological question. Here, we introduce the concept of single-cell multiomics which allows you capture multiple pieces of information (RNA, ATAC, protein expression) within a singular cell. Each modality comes with its own advantages and disadvantages that will determine which analyses you can perform with your data.

title: Single-cell Multiomics
text:
What is single-cell multiomics?
The field of single-cell sequencing has evolved beyond its intial focus on gene expression (RNA) capture. Additional methods have been developed to capture additional information for each cell, including the epigenome (chromatin accessibility), proteome, and more. Experiments that contain more than one modality is what is typically referred to a multiomics experiment.
Two of the most popular protocols that captures all three RNA, ATAC, and protein are ASAP-seq and TEA-seq. This then begs the question, when is it appropriate to use which modality? Kim et. al (2024) summarized the main principles and use cases for each modality. Here, we summarize the key points to serve as a reference for which modality best suits the experimental question or design that you may be using.



Table 1: Summary of common single-cell modalities.












scRNA-seq
scATAC-seq
ADT (surface protein)




Coverage
RNA abundance and splicing events
DNA chromatin accessibility and epigenetic regulation
Surface protein expression


Advantages
• Method of choice for transcriptional heterogeneity• Captures cell-to-cell expression variability
• Short sample prep time and works with few cells• Accessible and cost-effective
• Protein expression is not sparse• Insight into cell communication and signaling• Paired with RNA, better resolves cellular heterogeneity


Limitations
• Low capture efficiency and high dropout making data noisy, sparse, and variable• Incomplete genome coverage, especially in rare cell populations
• Non-specific antibody binding (background counts)• Composition bias from uneven capture efficiency
• Requires known antibodies (challening for non-model)


Applications
• Cell type identification• Cell subpopulation discovery• Gene expression dynamics• Cellular heterogeneity
• Cis/trans regulatory element analysis• Gene regulatory dynamics• Transcription factor activity• Epigenetic changes• Motif analsis
• Gene–protein correlation• Cell signaling pathways• Cell states and cell types

Project organization
When you have large amounts of data, it is easy to lose track of your files and become overwhelmed. We tend to prioritize the analysis and, in the excitement of getting a first look at our data, we often forget to consider how we are going to manage our data and files. This is a common mistake, as data management is often an afterthought when it should be a key part of the workflow from the very beginning. The HMS Data Management Working Group discusses in-depth some aspects to consider beyond the data creation and analysis.
One important aspect of data management is organization. For each experiment you work on and analyze data for, it is considered best practice to get organized by creating a planned storage space. We will do that for our analysis.

Mechanisms of HIV-1 persistence in the gut
Throughout this workshop, we will be utilizing a dataset from Wei et al. (2025). In this experiment, they ran DOGMA-seq on gut tissue from healthy samples and people living with HIV (PLWH) being treated with antiretroviral therapy (ART). As a result, they were able to characterize the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome of HIV-1 infected cells in contrast to healthy cells.
As a dataset that makes use of hashing (pooled samples), RNA, ATAC, and protein expression, this provides a great learning opportunity to experience how to process each of these modalities (Table 1).



Table 1: Modalities measured in the DOGMA-seq dataset.










Modality
Measures
Used for




Hashtag oligos (HTO)
Sample of origin
Demultiplexing pooled samples, doublet removal


RNA
Gene expression
Clustering, marker genes, cell type annotation


ATAC
Chromatin accessibility
Epigenomic profiles, transcription factor motifs


Antibody-derived tags (ADT)
Surface protein abundance
Validating cell types, protein markers







Key findings
In 2025, Wei et al. published results that showcased which factors promoted HIV-1 persistence in the gut. This study identified BACH2 as a key factor found in HIV-1 persistent T cells in the gut. The authors were able to identify this link across the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome by using the DOGMA-seq protocol (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Role of BACH2 in HIV-1 persistent T cells of the gut. Image source: Wei et al. (2025)

Samples
This dataset includes 17,642 cells in PLWH and 22,422 cells in HIV− individuals. Each PLWH donor was tagged with oligo-barcoded antibodies, pooled, and then sequenced. From all of these cells, the authors were able to identify 16 distinct cell types in the dataset (Figure 2).






Figure 2: UMAP of cell types identified in the samples collected. Image source: Wei et al. (2025)



To start, we will be using this heterogeneous population of cells to showcase how multiomics datasets are processed. We will first begin with the antibody hashes and protein expression before moving on to the ATAC-seq material.

Loading the dataset into Seurat
These samples were processed with 10X kits and were therefore processed with their propietary software. Here, we make use of two pipelines cellranger-arc and cellranger multi where the first processes RNA + ATAC and multi takes case of RNA + ADT.

Therefore, we will have two folders of results that we will eventually merged together into one singular Seurat object.
We will be starting with the ADT protein and RNA expression data for sample PT1.

# Sample of interest
sample <- "PT1"


Load counts matrix
First we will load in the counts matrices from the ADT folder with the Read10X() function. When we investigate the two matrices stored, we can see that we have both the “Gene Expression” (RNA) and “Antibody Capture” (ADT) matrices.

# Load raw counts data
counts <- Read10X(file.path("data", sample, "ADT"))
names(counts)

[1] "Gene Expression"  "Antibody Capture"


Seurat allows you to have Assays() where we can store different matrices for the same cells within a single object. To initialize our Seurat object, let us first use the CreateSeuratObject() function for the RNA expression. Note that we set assay = "RNA", which means that we can use the key “RNA” any time we want to look at the RNA expression over the protein or ATAC values.

# RNA expression matrix
counts_gex <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]

# Create seurat object
seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts_gex,
  assay = "RNA",
  project = sample)

seurat

Now we can see that we have created a Seurat object with 726385 cells and 36601 genes within the assay RNA.


Hashtags

# Protein expression matrix (ADT and HTO)
counts_adt <- counts[["Antibody Capture"]]

We can take a look at all the proteins included in our experiment by looking at the rownames of our counts matrix. In particular we are looking for any “protein” that begins with hashtag. Some runs are comprised of multiple, pooled samples that are tagged with specific antibodies. The way to identify which sample a cell comes from is to use these sequences to demultiplex. The first thing we are going to do here is pull out those antibodies and match them.

# Map of hash to patient
df_hash <- read.csv(file.path("data",
                              sample,
                              "ADT", "hashing_info.txt.gz"),
                    header = FALSE, sep = ":",
                    col.names = c("hash", "patient")) %>%
  # data wrangling
  mutate(hash = str_replace(hash, "H", "h"),
         hash = str_replace(hash, " ", ""))

rownames(counts_adt) <- str_replace_all(rownames(counts_adt), "_TotalA", "")

In the metadata, we see that there should only be 3 hashes, but we have 8 in our matrix. This is because the sequence for multiple hashes was included in the reference and does not effect the future results.
So we will remove the irrelevant hashes from our counts matrix.


Now that we have the names for each hash, we can pull those antibody captures out and store it as HTO in our Seurat object with the CreateAssayObject() function.

# Grab counts for just the hashes

k-medoids demultiplexing
HTODemux(): Run k-medoids clustering with positive.quantile = 0.95 to set a quantile threshold of 95% for a confident demultiplexing call.

https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/hashing_vignette.html
The demultiplexing function HTODemux() implements the following procedure: We perform a k-medoid clustering on the normalized HTO values, which initially separates cells into K(# of samples)+1 clusters. We calculate a ‘negative’ distribution for HTO. For each HTO, we use the cluster with the lowest average value as the negative group. For each HTO, we fit a negative binomial distribution to the negative cluster. We use the 0.99 quantile of this distribution as a threshold. Based on these thresholds, each cell is classified as positive or negative for each HTO. Cells that are positive for more than one HTOs are annotated as doublets.

# HTO demultiplexing
seurat <- HTODemux(
    seurat,
    assay = "HTO",
    positive.quantile = 0.99,
    verbose = TRUE)

HTODemux added the last six columns (17–21 in your list, plus HTO_maxID at 16):







Column
What it holds




HTO_maxID
The hashtag with the highest normalised signal in that cell, whether or not it passed the threshold.


HTO_secondID
The hashtag with the second-highest signal. Useful for seeing which two donors a doublet came from.


HTO_margin
The difference between the top and second hashtag’s normalised (CLR) values. Large means one hashtag clearly dominates; small means the cell is ambiguous.


HTO_classification
The detailed call. A singlet gets one hashtag name (hashtag2), a doublet gets both joined with _ (hashtag1_hashtag3), and a cell with no hashtag above threshold gets Negative.


HTO_classification.global
The detailed call collapsed into three groups: Singlet, Doublet or Negative. Filter on this one.


hash.ID
The final per-cell label: the hashtag name for singlets, and Doublet or Negative otherwise. HTODemux also sets the object’s active identities to this.

The majority of our remaining cells are identified as Negative, meaning that a conclusive label was unable to be determined from the data. These cells are typically empty or filled with ambient RNA and some hash counts. To evaluate if we truly believe these are low-quality cells to remove, we can assess the nCount_HTO to see how many hash counts are present in those cells. If the levels are very low, we will be unable to identify which patient the cell comes from, and therefore remove them.

VlnPlot(seurat,
        features = "nCount_HTO",
        group.by = "hash.ID",
        assay = "HTO",
        pt.size = 0) +
  scale_y_log10()

We can see why the cells that were called Negative received that label from the violin plot. Each cell had very low levels of hash expression, meaning that no algorithm would be able to confidently map the cell to a label.
We can also see patterns of expression for each hash across the identities. We are ideally looking for peaks of zero expression for hashes other than the hash.ID, indicating that the cell has high levels of the hash.ID hash.

  seurat,
  features = df_hash$hash,
  group.by = "hash.ID",

Figure 4: Ridge plot of HTO normalized expression for each hash.





Which is exactly what we see in the RidgePlot().


Removing doublets and negative
Now that we are confident in our demultiplexed calls, we can remove the identified doublets and negative cells. These will only introduce noise into the dataset so we will remove them from our analysis.

# Remove doublets and negatives
seurat_demux <- subset(seurat, subset = (hash.ID %in% df_hash$hash))
seurat_demux

An object of class Seurat 
36769 features across 4823 samples within 3 assays 
Active assay: HTO (3 features, 0 variable features)
 2 layers present: counts, data
 2 other assays present: RNA, ADT


And now we can take the mapping of hash to patient and add it to the metadata of our Seurat object. This way, moving forward, we are able to associate each cell with a specific patient. We will do a left_join() of to merge together this information.

# Add patient to metadata by matching hash
meta <- left_join(seurat_demux@meta.data,
                  df_hash, by = c("hash.ID" = "hash"))
rownames(meta) <- Cells(seurat_demux)

seurat_demux@meta.data <- meta

Oftentimes when you run left_join() of dataframes, you lose the rownames of the original dataframe. If we were to put this back into the Seurat object without the cell barcodes, we would get many errors in future steps. Hence why we explicitly set the rownames(meta) as a secondary step.

title: Generating Pooled Seurat Object
text:
Create Seurat object
First, we set up the script so that we can loop through multiple samples with a for loop. So we keep track of the sample names and create an empty list where we will store the Seurat objects. Additionally, as some of the datasets are pooled, we will need to run the demultiplexing steps for them in this step, so we create samples_pooled to keep track of which samples those are.

### Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(Seurat)
library(qs)
library(harmony)

### Metadata
df_meta <- read.csv("data_dogma_hiv/GSE299348/samples.tsv", sep = "\t")
rownames(df_meta) <- df_meta$library

### Load every dataset
# List of seurat object to eventually merge
list_seurat <- list()

# Note pooled samples to dehash later
samples_pooled <- c("PT1", "PT2", "PT3")

Next, we loop through each library in our metadata and build one Seurat object per sample. For every sample, the loop:

Selects real cells. We read the per_barcode_metrics.csv.gz file from the ATAC output of cellranger-arc and keep only the barcodes where is_cell == 1. This removes the empty droplets from the raw matrices so that the RNA and protein data contain the same set of cells as the ATAC data.
Creates the Seurat object. We load the counts from the ADT folder, subset the “Gene Expression” matrix to our cells, and create the RNA assay. We also record the patient and hiv_status from the metadata.
Separates hashtags from proteins. The “Antibody Capture” matrix holds both the hashtags and the surface proteins. For pooled samples, we read hashing_info.txt.gz and store only the hashtags used in that pool as the HTO assay. Every other antibody that is not a hashtag is stored as the ADT assay.
Demultiplexes pooled samples. For the samples in samples_pooled, we remove low-count cells, CLR-normalize the hashtags, and run HTODemux(), just as we did for PT1 in the previous lesson. We keep only the cells confidently assigned to a single hashtag and replace the patient column with the patient matched to that hashtag.
Stores the result. We prefix the patient IDs with patient_ so they are read as text rather than numbers, and add the object to list_seurat under the sample name.


# Loop through each sample
for (sample in df_meta$library) {
  
  print(sample)
  patient <- df_meta[sample, "patient"]
  hiv_status <- df_meta[sample, "hiv_status"]
  
  ### Get cells of interest
  cells <- read.csv(file.path("data_dogma_hiv/",
                              "GSE299348/", sample, 
                              "/ATAC/per_barcode_metrics.csv.gz")) %>%
    subset(is_cell == 1) %>%
    pull(barcode)

  ### Load counts
  counts <- Read10X(file.path("data_dogma_hiv",
                              "GSE299348",
                              sample,
                              "ADT"))
  
  ### RNA expression
  counts_gex <- counts[["Gene Expression"]]
  counts_gex <- counts_gex[, cells]
  
  ### Create seurat object
  seurat <- CreateSeuratObject(
    counts = counts_gex,
    assay = "RNA",
    project = sample)
  seurat$patient <- patient
  seurat$hiv_status <- hiv_status

  ### ADT and hashtags
  counts_anitbody <- counts[["Antibody Capture"]]
  counts_anitbody <- counts_anitbody[, cells]
  # Features all have _TotalA appended
  rownames(counts_anitbody) <- str_replace_all(rownames(counts_anitbody), "_TotalA", "")


  ### Hashtag counts
  # 8 hashtag sequences
  hashes <- paste0("hashtag", seq(1, 8))
  if (sample %in% samples_pooled) {
    df_hash <- read.csv(file.path("data_dogma_hiv",
                                  "GSE299348", sample,
                                  "ADT", "hashing_info.txt.gz"),
                        header = FALSE, sep = ":",
                        col.names = c("hash", "patient")) %>%
      # Fix capitalization and whitespace
      mutate(hash = str_replace(hash, "H", "h"),
             hash = str_replace(hash, " ", ""))

    # Hashtag matrix
    counts_hash <- counts_anitbody[df_hash$hash, Cells(seurat), drop = FALSE]
    seurat[["HTO"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_hash)
  }

  ### Protein counts
  counts_adt <- counts_anitbody[!rownames(counts_anitbody) %in% hashes, Cells(seurat)]
  seurat[["ADT"]] <- CreateAssayObject(counts = counts_adt)

  ### Demultiplex hashtags
  if (sample %in% samples_pooled) {
    seurat <- subset(seurat, nCount_ADT > 30)

    # CLR HTO normalization
    seurat <- NormalizeData(
      seurat,
      assay = "HTO",
      normalization.method = "CLR",
      margin = 2)

    # HTO demultiplexing
    seurat <- HTODemux(
      seurat,
      assay = "HTO",
      positive.quantile = 0.99,
      verbose = TRUE)

    # Remove negative and doublets (only keep confident hash)
    seurat <- subset(seurat, subset = hash.ID %in% df_hash$hash)
    seurat$patient <- df_hash$patient[match(seurat$hash.ID, df_hash$hash)]
  }

  # Turn patient column into string
  seurat$patient <- paste0("patient_", seurat$patient)

  # Store results in list
  list_seurat[[sample]] <- seurat

}

Now that we have create a Seurat object for each sample, we can now merge all datasets together. We can do this with the merge() and JoinLayers() function.

### Merge all datasets together
seurat <- merge(
  x = list_seurat[[1]], 
  y = list_seurat[2: length(list_seurat)],
  add.cell.ids = names(list_seurat)
)

Idents(seurat) <- "orig.ident"
DefaultAssay(seurat) <- "RNA"
seurat <- JoinLayers(seurat)

In the method section of the paper, they also mentioned that they removed cells with > 25% mitochondrial ratio to further clean up the dataset.

# Compute percent mito ratio
seurat$mitoRatio <- PercentageFeatureSet(object = seurat, pattern = "^MT-")
seurat$mitoRatio <- seurat@meta.data$mitoRatio / 100
seurat <- subset(seurat, mitoRatio < 0.25)

title: Generating Pooled Seurat Object
text:
Processing the Seurat object
With all the cells loaded, we can begin the standard processing steps. This entails:

Normalization
Variable feature selection
Scaling counts and running PCA
Assessing batch effect and running Harmony to integrate samples
UMAP
Shared nearest neighbors
Clustering


### Process RNA
DefaultAssay(seurat) <- "RNA"
seurat <- NormalizeData(seurat)
seurat <- FindVariableFeatures(seurat, nfeatures = 2000)
seurat <- ScaleData(seurat)
seurat <- RunPCA(seurat, npcs = 50, reduction.name = "pca_rna", verbose = FALSE)

seurat <- RunHarmony(seurat, group.by.vars = "orig.ident",
                     reduction.use = "pca_rna", dims.use = 1:30,
                     reduction.save = "harmony_rna", verbose = FALSE)
seurat <- RunUMAP(seurat, reduction = "harmony_rna", dims = 1:30,
                  reduction.name = "umap_rna", reduction.key = "rnaUMAP_",
                  verbose = FALSE)

seurat <- FindNeighbors(seurat, reduction = "harmony_rna", dims = 1:30,
                        graph.name = c("nn_rna", "snn_rna"), verbose = FALSE)
seurat <- FindClusters(seurat, graph.name = "snn_rna", resolution = 0.8,
                       cluster.name = "clusters_rna", verbose = FALSE)


UMAP visualizations
This takes us to the point of where we can load in our Seurat object:

# Load libraries and data
library(Seurat)
library(tidyverse)

seurat_demux <- readRDS("data/processed_seurat_objects/seurat_demux.RDS")

The UMAP coordinates were computed on the harmony corrected latent space, which we can visualize here to give a quick overview of if the integration was succesful.

DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "orig.ident",
        reduction = "umap_rna")







Figure 1: UMAP of the Harmony-integrated RNA expression, colored by sample.





We additionally clustered the cells at a resolution of 0.8

DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "snn_rna_res.0.8",
        reduction = "umap_rna",
        label = TRUE)

Single-cell Multiomics in R: Integrating RNA, Chromatin Accessibility, and Protein



Audience
Computational skills required
Duration




Biologists
Introduction to R
3-session online workshop (~9 hours of trainer-led time)




Description
This repository has teaching materials for a hands-on workshop on single-cell multiomics analysis in R. Single-cell multiomics experiments measure gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and surface proteins in the same cell, giving a far more complete picture of cell identity and gene regulation than any single assay can. Designed for wet lab scientists, this workshop walks through each modality using a real human gut tissue dataset, from raw counts to annotated cell types and analyses that combine all three. You will leave able to plan multiomics experiments with the analysis in mind, explore and interpret your own data, and have more productive conversations with bioinformaticians.
The workshop is organized into three parts, each taught in its own session:

Protein: Load the data, demultiplex pooled samples with hashtag oligos, and analyze surface protein (ADT) expression alongside RNA to annotate cell types.
Chromatin accessibility (ATAC): Process and explore single-cell ATAC-seq data to profile the epigenome of each cell.
Regulatory and joint analyses: Bring RNA, ATAC, and protein together to identify cell states and the regulatory programs that drive them.

We do not cover the upstream processing of scRNA-seq data in depth. If you are new to single-cell analysis, we recommend reviewing our Introduction to scRNA-seq workshop materials first.






Length of workshop



This workshop is taught as three 3-hour sessions, one for each part. Each part builds on the results of the previous one, so we recommend attending all three sessions in order.
These materials were developed for a trainer-led workshop, but are also amenable to self-guided learning.




Learning Objectives
In this workshop, the participants will:

Describe what single-cell multiomics measures and how to choose the right modalities for an experiment
Load Cell Ranger output into Seurat and demultiplex pooled samples using hashtag oligos (HTO)
Part 1: Protein

Normalize, visualize, and integrate surface protein (ADT) data
Annotate cell types using RNA and protein markers together

Part 2: Chromatin accessibility

Perform quality control and dimensionality reduction on single-cell ATAC-seq data
Explore chromatin accessibility across cell types

Part 3: Regulatory and joint analyses

Combine RNA, ATAC, and protein into a joint representation of each cell
Link accessible regions to genes and infer transcription factor activity




Lessons

Workshop schedule (trainer-led learning)
Self-learning

Applications
Download the most recent versions of R and RStudio for your laptop:

R (version 4.3.0 or above)
RStudio

Instructions for installing R packages




Install the packages in the order listed below.
All the package names listed below are case sensitive!
If you have a Mac, download and install this tool before installing your packages if using R versions 4.3.0 up to 4.4.3: gfortran-12.2. If you are using R versions after 4.4.3, install gfortran-14.2 instead.
At any point (especially if you’ve used R/Bioconductor in the past), in the console R may ask you if you want to update any old packages by asking Update all/some/none? [a/s/n]:. If you see this, type “a” at the prompt and hit Enter to update any old packages. Updating packages can sometimes take quite a bit of time to run, so please account for that before you start with these installations.
If you see a message in your console along the lines of “binary version available but the source version is later”, followed by a question, “Do you want to install from sources the package which needs compilation? y/n”, type n for no, and hit enter.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Learning objectives
In this lesson, we will:

Normalize protein counts with CLR and exclude isotype controls
Run PCA and UMAP on protein expression and correct library batch effects with Harmony
Compare RNA and protein expression to see how each modality resolves cell types
Annotate cell types using RNA and protein markers together

title: Protein Expression
text:
Overview of lesson
In this section, we will normalize the protein counts, reduce their dimensionality, and check whether the protein data alone separates our cells into sensible groups.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Protein expression (ADT)
Alongside RNA, each cell in our dataset was stained with a panel of 165 oligo-tagged antibodies, giving us a measure of surface protein abundance for every cell. Proteins are often the most direct readout of cell type.
Many of the markers used to define immune cell types (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, HLA-DR) were originally defined by their protein expression with flow cytometry.

# Set default assay to ADT
DefaultAssay(seurat_demux) <- "ADT"


Isotype controls
Not every antibody in the panel targets a human protein. Isotype controls are antibodies of the same class as the real antibodies but with no target in human cells. Any counts they receive come from non-specific binding, so they tell us the level of background noise in each cell. They are useful for quality control, but they carry no biological signal, so we will exclude them from the downstream analysis.
Our panel contains nine isotype controls:

# Isotype control antibodies in the panel
isotypes <- c("ArmenianHamsterIgG",
              "Mouse-IgG1-isotype", "Mouse-IgG2a-isotype", "Mouse-IgG2b-isotype",
              "RatIgG1k", "RatIgG1l", "RatIgG2a", "Rat-IgG2b-isotype", "RatIgG2c")

We can check the expression of each of these isotypes to confirm their expression levels.

# Isotype control expression by HIV status
VlnPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "hiv_status",
        features = isotypes,
        assay = "ADT",
        pt.size = 0)







Figure 1: Expression distribution of isotype controls in the protein panel.





We can see that there is pratically zero expression of each of these isotypes which confirms that we can proceed with our data as is.


Normalization
Antibody counts behave differently from RNA counts, which are typically log-normalized. Each antibody has its own background level, and a few highly abundant proteins can make up a large share of a cell’s counts. For this reason, we normalize with the centered log-ratio (CLR) transform, just as we did for the hashtags in the demultiplexing lesson. Setting margin = 2 normalizes each cell independently. As a result, each protein’s count is compared to the geometric mean of all the proteins in that cell.

# CLR normalization across proteins within each cell
seurat_demux <- NormalizeData(
  seurat_demux,
  normalization.method = "CLR",
  margin = 2)

seurat_demux

An object of class Seurat 
36774 features across 34984 samples within 3 assays 
Active assay: ADT (165 features, 0 variable features)
 2 layers present: counts, data
 2 other assays present: RNA, HTO
 3 dimensional reductions calculated: pca_rna, harmony_rna, umap_rna




Feature selection
Recall that our protein panel is comprised of 165 antibodies - which is a small number compared to the ~36,000 genes in the RNA assay. In a typical scRNA workflow, this would be where we identify the top variable genes in the datset. However, since there are so few protein, we will instead use every protein except the isotype controls.

# Use all proteins except the isotype controls
adt_features <- setdiff(rownames(seurat_demux[["ADT"]]), isotypes)
VariableFeatures(seurat_demux) <- adt_features

length(adt_features)

[1] 156


We are left with 156 proteins, which we scale before running PCA.

# Scale protein expression
seurat_demux <- ScaleData(seurat_demux)
seurat_demux

An object of class Seurat 
36774 features across 34984 samples within 3 assays 
Active assay: ADT (165 features, 156 variable features)
 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data
 2 other assays present: RNA, HTO
 3 dimensional reductions calculated: pca_rna, harmony_rna, umap_rna




PCA
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a method that allows us to summarize and reduce the dimensions of our dataset to emphasize the variation and similarity of our data. Utilizing PCA, we are able to identify strong patterns in our dataset to group cells together.

Calculating PCA






Video on how PCA is calculated





For a more detailed explanation on PCA, please look over this lesson (adapted from StatQuests/Josh Starmer’s YouTube video). We also strongly encourage you to explore the video StatQuest’s video for a more thorough understanding.



Let’s say you are working with a single-cell RNA-seq dataset with 12,000 cells and you have quantified the expression of 20,000 genes. The schematic below demonstrates how you would go from a cell-by-gene matrix to principal component (PC) scores for each individual cell. This same principle applies for the ADT assay, except we use protein instead of genes.






Figure 2: Schematic of PCA: from a cell-by-gene count matrix to principal component scores per cell.



Now that we have a general idea of what the PCA calculation does, we can compute pca_adt using the RunPCA() function. At this step, we will also set the reduction.name to ensure that we can keep track of which assay a calculation was computed on.

# PCA on protein expression
seurat_demux <- RunPCA(
  seurat_demux,
  npcs = 30,
  assay = "ADT",
  reduction.name = "pca_adt",
  reduction.key = "adtPC_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)



Visualizing PCA
Principal components analysis (PCA) stratifies the data by variance. Points closer together are more similar, and points further apart are more dissimilar. We can visualize the PCA results using DimPlot() to see if we can identify if there is any technical or biological variable is driving the separation of cells.

# Protein PCA by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "pca_adt",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 3: Protein PCA colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





The libraries are spread out along the first principal component: PT1 forms its own group at one end, PT4 sits at the other, and PT2 occupies its own region at the top of the plot. In this dataset, HIV status and library are confounded. Every PLWH cell comes from one of the four pooled PT libraries. Therefore, we cannot yet tell how much of this separation is biology and how much is a technical difference between sequencing runs. We will keep an eye on this in the UMAP.


PCA weights
We can additionally see which proteins have the highest weights (positive and negative) for each principal component. Ideally, we would hope to see cell type markers at this point.

# Top proteins for the first 5 PCs
print(seurat_demux[["pca_adt"]],
      dims = 1:5, nfeatures = 5)

adtPC_ 1 
Positive:  CD279, CD134, CD83, LOX-1, CD74 
Negative:  IgM, CD69, HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD11a, CD8 
adtPC_ 2 
Positive:  CD38, CD63, CD47, CD44, CD9 
Negative:  CD2, CD7, CD3, CD5, CD4 
adtPC_ 3 
Positive:  HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD22, HLA-DR, CD35, CD21 
Negative:  CD2, CD69, CD7, CD45, CD3 
adtPC_ 4 
Positive:  HLA-DR, HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD22, CD35, CD150 
Negative:  CD63, CD38, CD48, CD49d, CD137 
adtPC_ 5 
Positive:  CD196, CD9, CD163, CD23, CD56 
Negative:  CD45, CD19, CD48, CD22, CD21 


The later PCs look like cell type markers. adtPC_2 separates T cells (CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7). adtPC_3 and adtPC_4 are driven by B cell markers (CD21, CD22, CD35, HLA-DR). adtPC_1, however, mixes markers from many lineages, which fits with it separating libraries rather than cell types.



UMAP
UMAP takes the information from the top PCs and arranges the cells in two dimensions while trying to preserve local structure. Cells that are close together have similar protein expression based upon the values stored in the principle components. Bear in mind that the distances between clusters should not be over-interpreted.
First, we run UMAP directly on the uncorrected PCA.

# UMAP on uncorrected protein PCA
seurat_demux <- RunUMAP(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "pca_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  reduction.name = "umap_adt_uncorrected",
  reduction.key = "adtUncorrectedUMAP_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)

Now we can assess if the batch effect we identified in the PCA section is present in the UMAP.

# Protein UMAP before integration by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "umap_adt_uncorrected",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 4: Protein UMAP before integration, colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





The batch effect is much clearer in the UMAP. Nearly all cells from PT2 and PT3 form a separate island, and PT1 and PT4 each occupy their own region instead of mixing with the HIV− libraries. Since we expect the same immune cell types to be present in every library, this is a strong sign that we need to run integration. As we did for RNA, we set group.by.vars = "orig.ident" to correct for differences between libraries.


Harmony integration
If cells cluster by sample, batch, dataset, or modality, integration can greatly improve the clustering and downstream analyses. We “integrate” or “harmonize” the groups to overlay cells that share a common set of biological features. We use Harmony, which iteratively adjusts the principal components so that cells of the same type from different libraries are placed together.

# Correct protein PCs for library
seurat_demux <- RunHarmony(
  seurat_demux,
  group.by.vars = "orig.ident",
  reduction.use = "pca_adt",
  dims.use = 1:20,
  reduction.save = "harmony_adt",
  verbose = FALSE)

# UMAP on corrected protein PCs
seurat_demux <- RunUMAP(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "harmony_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  reduction.name = "umap_adt",
  reduction.key = "adtUMAP_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)

We use this corrected space as the input to re-run UMAP, which we can now visualize here:

# Protein UMAP after integration by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "umap_adt",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 5: Protein UMAP after Harmony integration, colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





After Harmony, cells from every library are well mixed across the UMAP and no library forms its own island.






Over-correction



Because HIV status is confounded with library, correcting for library also removes any protein differences that are truly driven by HIV status. This is an acceptable tradeoff for visualizing cell types, but we should not use the integrated embedding to compare PLWH and HIV− cells.




Clustering
Now that we have an integrated protein embedding, we can group the cells into clusters based on their protein expression alone. Clustering is a graph-based approach that happens in two steps:

FindNeighbors(): Build a k-nearest neighbor graph, connecting each cell to the cells with the most similar protein expression. We use the Harmony-corrected PCs (harmony_adt) and the same 20 dimensions we used for the UMAP. Following the convention from the RNA analysis, we name the graphs nn_adt and snn_adt so that they do not overwrite the RNA graphs.
FindClusters(): Partition the shared nearest neighbor graph (snn_adt) into clusters. The resolution sets the granularity: smaller values give fewer, larger clusters.


# Build the nearest neighbor graph on corrected protein PCs
seurat_demux <- FindNeighbors(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "harmony_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  graph.name = c("nn_adt", "snn_adt"),
  verbose = FALSE)

# Cluster the cells at a resolution of 0.8
seurat_demux <- FindClusters(
  seurat_demux,
  graph.name = "snn_adt",
  resolution = 0.8,
  random.seed = 123456789L,
  verbose = FALSE)

 2 other assays present: RNA, HTO
 3 dimensional reductions calculated: pca_rna, harmony_rna, umap_rna

title: Protein Expression
text:
Feature selection
Recall that our protein panel is comprised of 165 antibodies - which is a small number compared to the ~36,000 genes in the RNA assay. In a typical scRNA workflow, this would be where we identify the top variable genes in the datset. However, since there are so few protein, we will instead use every protein except the isotype controls.

# Use all proteins except the isotype controls
adt_features <- setdiff(rownames(seurat_demux[["ADT"]]), isotypes)
VariableFeatures(seurat_demux) <- adt_features

length(adt_features)

[1] 156


We are left with 156 proteins, which we scale before running PCA.

# Scale protein expression
seurat_demux <- ScaleData(seurat_demux)
seurat_demux

An object of class Seurat 
36774 features across 34984 samples within 3 assays 
Active assay: ADT (165 features, 156 variable features)
 3 layers present: counts, data, scale.data
 2 other assays present: RNA, HTO
 3 dimensional reductions calculated: pca_rna, harmony_rna, umap_rna

title: Protein Expression
text:
PCA
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a method that allows us to summarize and reduce the dimensions of our dataset to emphasize the variation and similarity of our data. Utilizing PCA, we are able to identify strong patterns in our dataset to group cells together.

Calculating PCA






Video on how PCA is calculated





For a more detailed explanation on PCA, please look over this lesson (adapted from StatQuests/Josh Starmer’s YouTube video). We also strongly encourage you to explore the video StatQuest’s video for a more thorough understanding.



Let’s say you are working with a single-cell RNA-seq dataset with 12,000 cells and you have quantified the expression of 20,000 genes. The schematic below demonstrates how you would go from a cell-by-gene matrix to principal component (PC) scores for each individual cell. This same principle applies for the ADT assay, except we use protein instead of genes.






Figure 2: Schematic of PCA: from a cell-by-gene count matrix to principal component scores per cell.



Now that we have a general idea of what the PCA calculation does, we can compute pca_adt using the RunPCA() function. At this step, we will also set the reduction.name to ensure that we can keep track of which assay a calculation was computed on.

# PCA on protein expression
seurat_demux <- RunPCA(
  seurat_demux,
  npcs = 30,
  assay = "ADT",
  reduction.name = "pca_adt",
  reduction.key = "adtPC_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)



Visualizing PCA
Principal components analysis (PCA) stratifies the data by variance. Points closer together are more similar, and points further apart are more dissimilar. We can visualize the PCA results using DimPlot() to see if we can identify if there is any technical or biological variable is driving the separation of cells.

# Protein PCA by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "pca_adt",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 3: Protein PCA colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





The libraries are spread out along the first principal component: PT1 forms its own group at one end, PT4 sits at the other, and PT2 occupies its own region at the top of the plot. In this dataset, HIV status and library are confounded. Every PLWH cell comes from one of the four pooled PT libraries. Therefore, we cannot yet tell how much of this separation is biology and how much is a technical difference between sequencing runs. We will keep an eye on this in the UMAP.


PCA weights
We can additionally see which proteins have the highest weights (positive and negative) for each principal component. Ideally, we would hope to see cell type markers at this point.

# Top proteins for the first 5 PCs
print(seurat_demux[["pca_adt"]],
      dims = 1:5, nfeatures = 5)

adtPC_ 1 
Positive:  CD279, CD134, CD83, LOX-1, CD74 
Negative:  IgM, CD69, HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD11a, CD8 
adtPC_ 2 
Positive:  CD38, CD63, CD47, CD44, CD9 
Negative:  CD2, CD7, CD3, CD5, CD4 
adtPC_ 3 
Positive:  HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD22, HLA-DR, CD35, CD21 
Negative:  CD2, CD69, CD7, CD45, CD3 
adtPC_ 4 
Positive:  HLA-DR, HLA-DR-DP-DQ, CD22, CD35, CD150

adtPC_ 5

Negative:  CD45, CD19, CD48, CD22, CD21 


The later PCs look like cell type markers. adtPC_2 separates T cells (CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7). adtPC_3 and adtPC_4 are driven by B cell markers (CD21, CD22, CD35, HLA-DR). adtPC_1, however, mixes markers from many lineages, which fits with it separating libraries rather than cell types.

title: Protein Expression
text:
UMAP
UMAP takes the information from the top PCs and arranges the cells in two dimensions while trying to preserve local structure. Cells that are close together have similar protein expression based upon the values stored in the principle components. Bear in mind that the distances between clusters should not be over-interpreted.
First, we run UMAP directly on the uncorrected PCA.

# UMAP on uncorrected protein PCA
seurat_demux <- RunUMAP(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "pca_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  reduction.name = "umap_adt_uncorrected",
  reduction.key = "adtUncorrectedUMAP_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)

Now we can assess if the batch effect we identified in the PCA section is present in the UMAP.

# Protein UMAP before integration by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "umap_adt_uncorrected",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 4: Protein UMAP before integration, colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





The batch effect is much clearer in the UMAP. Nearly all cells from PT2 and PT3 form a separate island, and PT1 and PT4 each occupy their own region instead of mixing with the HIV− libraries. Since we expect the same immune cell types to be present in every library, this is a strong sign that we need to run integration. As we did for RNA, we set group.by.vars = "orig.ident" to correct for differences between libraries.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Harmony integration
If cells cluster by sample, batch, dataset, or modality, integration can greatly improve the clustering and downstream analyses. We “integrate” or “harmonize” the groups to overlay cells that share a common set of biological features. We use Harmony, which iteratively adjusts the principal components so that cells of the same type from different libraries are placed together.

# Correct protein PCs for library
seurat_demux <- RunHarmony(
  seurat_demux,
  group.by.vars = "orig.ident",
  reduction.use = "pca_adt",
  dims.use = 1:20,
  reduction.save = "harmony_adt",
  verbose = FALSE)

# UMAP on corrected protein PCs
seurat_demux <- RunUMAP(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "harmony_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  reduction.name = "umap_adt",
  reduction.key = "adtUMAP_",
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed.use = 123456789L)

We use this corrected space as the input to re-run UMAP, which we can now visualize here:

# Protein UMAP after integration by library and HIV status
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = c("orig.ident", "hiv_status"),
        reduction = "umap_adt",
        shuffle = TRUE)







Figure 5: Protein UMAP after Harmony integration, colored by library (left) and HIV status (right).





After Harmony, cells from every library are well mixed across the UMAP and no library forms its own island.






Over-correction



Because HIV status is confounded with library, correcting for library also removes any protein differences that are truly driven by HIV status. This is an acceptable tradeoff for visualizing cell types, but we should not use the integrated embedding to compare PLWH and HIV− cells.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Comparing to RNA clusters
Earlier, we clustered the cells on their RNA expression at a resolution of 0.8 (stored in the snn_rna_res.0.8 column). A useful check is to color the protein UMAP by these RNA clusters: if both modalities capture the same cell types, each RNA cluster should occupy its own region of the protein UMAP.

DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "snn_rna_res.0.8",
        reduction = "umap_adt",
        label = TRUE,
        seed = 123456789L)







Figure 3: Protein UMAP colored by the RNA clusters at a resolution of 0.8.





Some RNA clusters, such as 15 and 17, map to distinct regions of the protein UMAP, and clusters 4 and 10 share a region. Many of the remaining clusters, however, overlap heavily. The protein panel resolves the major immune lineages well but cannot distinguish all the finer populations that RNA identifies. This shows that each modality captures different information about a cell, which is why combining them can give a more complete picture than either one alone.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Cell typing
Now that we have both RNA and protein measurements for every cell, we can use them together to assign a cell type to each RNA cluster. We use a set of known marker genes for the cell populations expected in the human gut. For many of the immune populations, our antibody panel also contains a matching protein, which gives us a second, independent line of evidence.

Notice that the protein column is empty for the non-immune cell types. The antibody panel was designed to profile immune cells, so for the epithelial and stromal populations we have to rely on RNA alone.

Identifying CD4+ and CD8+ T cells
T cells are a good example of why it helps to have both modalities. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are traditionally separated by the surface proteins CD4 and CD8. In scRNA-seq, however, the CD4 transcript is notoriously hard to detect: it is expressed at low levels, so many CD4+ T cells have zero CD4 counts in the data. This is known as dropout.
To see this, we plot the RNA and protein expression of CD4 and CD8 side by side on the RNA UMAP. Since the same feature name (e.g. CD4) exists in both the RNA and ADT assays, we add the assay key as a prefix (rna_ or adt_) to tell Seurat which one to plot.

# CD4 and CD8 expression from RNA and protein
FeaturePlot(seurat_demux,
            features = c("rna_CD4", "rna_CD8A", "adt_CD4", "adt_CD8"),
            reduction = "umap_rna",
            order = TRUE,
            ncol = 2)







Figure 8: RNA (top) and protein (bottom) expression of CD4 and CD8 on the RNA UMAP.





The two modalities tell a consistent story, but with very different clarity:

RNA: CD4 transcripts are detected in only a scattered subset of cells in the CD4 T cell region (about 7% of cells in cluster 1 and 12% in cluster 11). CD8A is detected more often, but still in only about a quarter of the cells in the CD8 T cell cluster (cluster 3).
Protein: CD4 and CD8 protein light up almost the entire CD4 and CD8 T cell regions, respectively. Because antibody counts are much higher than the counts for a single transcript, the protein signal does not suffer from the same dropout.

If we only had the RNA, we would identify CD4 T cells from the other markers in the table (CD3E, IL7R, CD40LG). With the protein, we have direct confirmation of the marker that defines the population.






CD4 on monocytes



You may notice moderate CD4 protein (and some CD4 RNA) in the small monocyte cluster as well. This is real biology: human monocytes express low levels of CD4. This is why we use a combination of markers, rather than a single one, to assign cell types.




Assigning cell types
Using the marker genes and proteins, we assigned a cell type to each of the 20 RNA clusters. For clusters where the markers were less clear-cut, we have left a comment explaining the decision.

Protein vs RNA Expression
Earlier, we saw that CD4 protein marks the CD4 T cells much more clearly than the CD4 transcript. To look at this more closely, we can compare the RNA and protein expression of CD4 in each individual cell, split by cell type.

ggplot(df_cd4) +

There are a few things to notice in this plot:

Most cells have zero CD4 RNA, even the CD4 T cells. In every panel, the majority of points sit in a vertical line at x = 0. In the CD4 T cells, 92% of cells have no CD4 transcripts detected, yet these cells still have a wide range of CD4 protein values.
The protein separates the CD4 T cells from the rest. The CD4 T cell panel has the highest CD4 protein values, followed by the CD14 monocytes, which express low levels of CD4. In most other cell types, half or more of the cells have no CD4 protein counts at all.
Protein is never completely clean. Every cell type has some cells with low to moderate CD4 protein. This is the non-specific background binding we discussed with the isotype controls, and it is why we look at the relative level of a protein between cell types rather than treating any non-zero value as “positive”.

Together, these show why the two modalities complement each other: RNA measures thousands of genes but misses many lowly expressed transcripts, while protein measures far fewer features but detects the ones in the panel more consistently.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Clustering
Now that we have an integrated protein embedding, we can group the cells into clusters based on their protein expression alone. Clustering is a graph-based approach that happens in two steps:

FindNeighbors(): Build a k-nearest neighbor graph, connecting each cell to the cells with the most similar protein expression. We use the Harmony-corrected PCs (harmony_adt) and the same 20 dimensions we used for the UMAP. Following the convention from the RNA analysis, we name the graphs nn_adt and snn_adt so that they do not overwrite the RNA graphs.
FindClusters(): Partition the shared nearest neighbor graph (snn_adt) into clusters. The resolution sets the granularity: smaller values give fewer, larger clusters. We use a resolution of 0.8 so that we can compare directly to the RNA clusters.


# Build the nearest neighbor graph on corrected protein PCs
seurat_demux <- FindNeighbors(
  seurat_demux,
  reduction = "harmony_adt",
  dims = 1:20,
  graph.name = c("nn_adt", "snn_adt"),
  verbose = FALSE)

# Cluster the cells at a resolution of 0.8
seurat_demux <- FindClusters(
  seurat_demux,
  graph.name = "snn_adt",
  resolution = 0.8,
  random.seed = 123456789L,
  verbose = FALSE)

The cluster assignments are stored in the metadata in a column named after the graph and resolution, snn_adt_res.0.8, which sits alongside the RNA clusters in snn_rna_res.0.8.






Active identities



FindClusters() also sets the active identities, Idents(seurat_demux), and the seurat_clusters column to the clusters it just computed. The RNA clusters are still stored safely in snn_rna_res.0.8, but keep in mind that seurat_clusters now holds the protein clusters.


We can visualize the protein clusters on the protein UMAP:

# Protein clusters on the protein UMAP
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "snn_adt_res.0.8",
        reduction = "umap_adt",
        label = TRUE)







Figure 6: Protein UMAP colored by the protein clusters at a resolution of 0.8.

title: Protein Expression
text:
Comparing RNA and ADT
We now have two independent sets of clusters at the same resolution: one computed from RNA expression (snn_rna_res.0.8) and one from protein expression (snn_adt_res.0.8). Let’s start by plotting each set of clusters on the UMAP of its own modality, side by side.

# RNA clusters on the RNA UMAP
p_rna <- DimPlot(seurat_demux,
                 group.by = "snn_rna_res.0.8",
                 reduction = "umap_rna",
                 label = TRUE) +
  ggtitle("RNA clusters")

# Protein clusters on the protein UMAP
p_adt <- DimPlot(seurat_demux,
                 group.by = "snn_adt_res.0.8",
                 reduction = "umap_adt",
                 label = TRUE) +
  ggtitle("Protein clusters")

# Plot side by side
p_rna + p_adt







Figure 6: RNA clusters on the RNA UMAP (left) and protein clusters on the protein UMAP (right), both at a resolution of 0.8.





Even at the same resolution, the two modalities organize the cells quite differently. On the RNA UMAP, the clusters form well-separated islands, with clear gaps between the major groups. On the protein UMAP, most of the cells form one continuous structure. This difference comes from what each modality measures. RNA clustering uses 2,000 variable genes, which capture many cell type-specific programs, while protein clustering uses our panel of about 150 surface markers. Cells that share most of their surface markers end up close together in protein space, even if their transcriptomes are distinct.
Earlier, we clustered the cells on their RNA expression at a resolution of 0.8 (stored in the snn_rna_res.0.8 column). A useful check is to color the protein UMAP by these RNA clusters: if both modalities capture the same cell types, each RNA cluster should occupy its own region of the protein UMAP.

# RNA clusters on the protein UMAP
DimPlot(seurat_demux,
        group.by = "snn_rna_res.0.8",
        reduction = "umap_adt",
        label = TRUE)







Figure 7: Protein UMAP colored by the RNA clusters at a resolution of 0.8.





When we look at the proteins on panel, we can see that they are primarily associated with immune popluations. As a result, the protein expression alone is not capable of identifying populations such as epithelial cells. This shows that each modality captures different information about a cell, which is why combining them can give a more complete picture than either one alone.
